MOLECULE 1 | RECORDS C14  
ANALYSIS: Phytoene is a C40 carotenoid hydrocarbon with a long isoprenoid chain, and the human compartmental-model estimate of 58% bioavailability is affirmative high-threshold evidence for a lipophilic isoprenoid. However, phytoene lacks the polar quinone head of the query and is a more flexible, less rigid hydrocarbon; its high estimate may reflect tracer modeling and a different micellar/chylomicron partitioning profile. It is relevant but only moderately transferable to CoQ10.

MOLECULE 2 | RECORDS C02  
ANALYSIS: This is the same phytoene evidence expressed as 58.5 ± 18.9% absolute bioavailability in humans. It is the strongest high-bioavailability counterexample among the isoprenoid records. Still, phytoene is structurally distinct from CoQ10: it is a nonpolar C40 carotenoid precursor, whereas CoQ10 has a substituted benzoquinone head and a longer, largely saturated polyisoprenoid tail. The high value supports the possibility that some large isoprenoids can be well absorbed, but it does not directly establish high CoQ10 bioavailability.

MOLECULE 3 | RECORDS C11  
ANALYSIS: Mulberroside A is a glycoside whose low oral bioavailability is attributed to rapid bacterial deglycosylation. This mechanism is not relevant to CoQ10, which has no sugar moiety and is not subject to the same first-pass intestinal metabolism. This record provides essentially no transferable evidence for the query.

MOLECULE 4 | RECORDS C03, C07, C22, C13, C06, C04, C24, C17  
ANALYSIS: Lycopene is the most extensively documented carotenoid here. Several human systemic-availability measurements are clearly below 20%: 0.17% from tomato paste, ~0.2–0.3% from pureed tomato, ~1.2% from synthetic lycopene in oil, and ~2.6% from capsules. These are affirmative low-threshold results for a large, highly lipophilic isoprenoid. In contrast, isotope-tracer studies report 12–24% absorption, with all-trans lycopene at 23.2% and cis-lycopene at 24.5%, which are above the threshold. The higher values likely reflect labeled absorption into plasma/chylomicrons rather than classical absolute systemic bioavailability and are formulation/matrix dependent. For CoQ10, the low lycopene values are more transferable because CoQ10 also has a large lipophilic isoprenoid body and poor aqueous solubility, although CoQ10’s quinone head and saturated side chain differ from lycopene’s conjugated hydrocarbon.

MOLECULE 5 | RECORDS C23  
ANALYSIS: This record reports 24.5% bioavailability for cis-lycopene isomers in healthy adults. It is another high-threshold carotenoid result, but cis-isomers are known to be more bioaccessible than all-trans forms. CoQ10 is not a carotenoid and does not have the same cis/trans isomer considerations. This evidence is only weakly transferable and does not outweigh the low lycopene systemic-availability measurements.

MOLECULE 6 | RECORDS C12  
ANALYSIS: Tocotrienol-rich palm oil has poor oral bioavailability in humans. Tocotrienol is structurally closer to CoQ10 than the carotenoids are: it has a polar chromanol head group attached to an isoprenoid tail, similar in amphipathic character to CoQ10’s quinone-plus-polyisoprenyl structure. This is affirmative low-threshold evidence from a related lipophilic isoprenoid and is the most transferable supportive record for a low CoQ10 prediction.

MOLECULE 7 | RECORDS C10  
ANALYSIS: Hyperforin shows high oral bioavailability from an extract, but it is a prenylated phloroglucinol with a much smaller molecular size and different physicochemical behavior than CoQ10. Its high bioavailability does not translate well to a large, poorly water-soluble ubiquinone. This record is not strong enough to support a high prediction.

MOLECULE 8 | RECORDS C01, C26, C25, C20, C21, C16, C05, C18, C09, C19  
ANALYSIS: Mycophenolate mofetil is a small-molecule ester prodrug with near-complete oral bioavailability. It shares no relevant structural or physicochemical features with CoQ10. These records are not transferable to the query.

MOLECULE 9 | RECORDS C27  
ANALYSIS: BI 425809 is a synthetic small-molecule drug with 71.64% absolute bioavailability. It is not structurally related to CoQ10 and its absorption properties do not inform the query.

MOLECULE 10 | RECORDS C15, C08  
ANALYSIS: Nabumetone is a small lipophilic drug with 38% absolute bioavailability in healthy subjects and 32% systemic availability in cirrhosis patients. It is not an isoprenoid lipid and has no relevant absorption mechanism in common with CoQ10. This evidence is not transferable.

FINAL CALIBRATION  
DIRECT EVIDENCE BALANCE: The strongest low-threshold evidence comes from human lycopene systemic-availability measurements (0.17–2.6%) and from tocotrienol, a structurally close isoprenoid with poor oral bioavailability. The strongest high-threshold evidence comes from phytoene (58%) and labeled lycopene absorption estimates (23–24%). The low lycopene values are direct systemic-availability measurements, while the high lycopene values are tracer-based absorption estimates; phytoene is a less direct structural analog. On balance, the affirmative low evidence is more directly relevant to CoQ10.

TRANSFERABILITY CHECK: Tocotrienol transfers best because it shares the polar-head-plus-isoprenoid-tail architecture and poor water solubility of CoQ10. Lycopene transfers moderately as a large lipophilic isoprenoid, especially the low systemic-availability results. Phytoene transfers less well because it is a nonpolar hydrocarbon with no polar head and may have better micellar solubilization. MMF, hyperforin, BI 425809, and nabumetone are not transferable.

QUERY-SPECIFIC CHECK: The query is recognized as coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone-10) from the dimethoxy-methylbenzoquinone core and decaprenyl side chain. Its established oral bioavailability behavior is known to be low and formulation-dependent due to high molecular weight, extreme lipophilicity, and poor aqueous solubility. This is consistent with the low prediction.

THRESHOLD DECISION: The weight of transferable experimental evidence supports F < 20%, so the prediction is low.

ANALYSIS: This is the same phytoene evidence expressed as 58.5 ± 18.9% absolute bioavailability in humans. It is the strongest high-bioavailability counterexample among the isoprenoid records. Still, phytoene is structurally distinct from CoQ10: it is a nonpolar C40 carotenoid precursor, whereas CoQ10 has a substituted benzoquinone head and a longer, largely saturated polyisoprenoid tail. The high value supports the possibility that some large isoprenoids can be well absorbed, but it does not directly establish high CoQ10 bioavailability.

MOLECULE 3 | RECORDS C11  
ANALYSIS: Mulberroside A is a glycoside whose low oral bioavailability is attributed to rapid bacterial deglycosylation. This mechanism is not relevant to CoQ10, which has no sugar moiety and is not subject to the same first-pass intestinal metabolism. This record provides essentially no transferable evidence for the query.

MOLECULE 4 | RECORDS C03, C07, C22, C13, C06, C04, C24, C17  
ANALYSIS: Lycopene is the most extensively documented carotenoid here. Several human systemic-availability measurements are clearly below 20%: 0.17% from tomato paste, ~0.2–0.3% from pureed tomato, ~1.2% from synthetic lycopene in oil, and ~2.6% from capsules. These are affirmative low-threshold results for a large, highly lipophilic isoprenoid. In contrast, isotope-tracer studies report 12–24% absorption, with all-trans lycopene at 23.2% and cis-lycopene at 24.5%, which are above the threshold. The higher values likely reflect labeled absorption into plasma/chylomicrons rather than classical absolute systemic bioavailability and are formulation/matrix dependent. For CoQ10, the low lycopene values are more transferable because CoQ10 also has a large lipophilic isoprenoid body and poor aqueous solubility, although CoQ10’s quinone head and saturated side chain differ from lycopene’s conjugated hydrocarbon.

MOLECULE 5 | RECORDS C23  
ANALYSIS: This record reports 24.5% bioavailability for cis-lycopene isomers in healthy adults. It is another high-threshold carotenoid result, but cis-isomers are known to be more bioaccessible than all-trans forms. CoQ10 is not a carotenoid and does not have the same cis/trans isomer considerations. This evidence is only weakly transferable and does not outweigh the low lycopene systemic-availability measurements.

MOLECULE 6 | RECORDS C12  
ANALYSIS: Tocotrienol-rich palm oil has poor oral bioavailability in humans. Tocotrienol is structurally closer to CoQ10 than the carotenoids are: it has a polar chromanol head group attached to an isoprenoid tail, similar in amphipathic character to CoQ10’s quinone-plus-polyisoprenyl structure. This is affirmative low-threshold evidence from a related lipophilic isoprenoid and is the most transferable supportive record for a low CoQ10 prediction.

MOLECULE 7 | RECORDS C10  
ANALYSIS: Hyperforin shows high oral bioavailability from an extract, but it is a prenylated phloroglucinol with a much smaller molecular size and different physicochemical behavior than CoQ10.
